summary: This experimental memo describes the Internet Route Access Protocol, an open distance vector routing protocol meant for all levels of the Internet, from single local networks to the major routers of a large network provider.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers need to learn which roads lead where. This paper proposes one way for them to share that information, small networks and big ones alike.

questions: what is rap route access protocol
distance vector routing across network scales
how does rap handle routing metrics
subtitle: An open distance-vector routing protocol for all scales of the Internet

tldr.problem: Existing routing protocols are specialized for either small networks (like RIP) or large inter-domain networks (like BGP). No single protocol scales effectively from private LANs to international carrier networks, nor do they work well when networks cross organizational boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: RAP is a distance-vector protocol that operates on TCP port 38 and UDP port 38. Routers exchange complete route information and then send only updates. Routes carry rich metrics (bandwidth, delay, cost) and policy options, allowing routers to use flexible policies at any scale.
tldr.outcome: RAP enables routers at any level of the Internet to exchange routing information using a single protocol, with support for complex policies, aggregation, and scaling from LANs to international backbones.

today: RFC 1476 is Experimental and was never deployed. BGP evolved to serve inter-domain routing and OSPF for interior routing, making RAP obsolete. The author's vision of a single protocol scaling across all routing levels was not realized, though modern protocols like OSPF and BGP have become more flexible and capable.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RAP (Internet Route Access Protocol) is an open distance-vector routing protocol designed for use at all scales of the Internet, from isolated LANs to major international carrier networks. Unlike existing protocols, RAP does not distinguish strictly between interior routing (within an organization) and exterior routing (between organizations), allowing routes to be shared more freely.

The protocol aims to maximize the dissemination of topology information, aggregating routes only when bandwidth, thrust, or policy constraints require it. This philosophy enables aggressive optimization of routes where desired, without the restrictions of protocols with strict hierarchical area definitions. RAP operates over both IPv4 and IPv7 networks while using IPv7 addressing internally.
sections.plainLanguage: RAP is one routing protocol that scales from a small office network to the entire Internet. It lets routers share more information and make smarter choices about which path to take.

sections.title: Why Distance Vector Scales
sections.content:
Routing algorithms fall into two classes: link-state and distance-vector. Link-state protocols like OSPF require each router to build a complete map of the network topology. This works well for small, well-defined areas, but becomes impractical at scale when the entire network topology is too large and volatile to map completely.

Distance-vector protocols like RIP and BGP work by having each router ask its neighbors for their best routes, then choosing the best routes to advertise further. This approach has proven to scale from small LANs (RIP) to inter-domain networks (BGP), suggesting that distance-vector can handle the full range. RAP extends this insight, applying distance-vector uniformly across all scales rather than using different protocols for different scopes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routing is link-state, where routers build a complete map. Others are distance-vector, where routers just ask neighbors. Distance-vector works at both tiny and huge scales, so RAP uses it everywhere.

sections.title: Protocol Format and Commands
sections.content:
RAP operates on TCP port 38 (for peer-to-peer routing exchange) and UDP port 38 (for peer discovery). RAP commands carry a header with a length field, a version number, and a command code. For TCP, the length field marks the boundary between commands in the stream. For UDP, each datagram contains exactly one command.

RAP defines five simple command types. The No-operation command resets the peer's keepalive timer and announces the sender is running RAP. A Poll command requests that the other side respond without delay. The Error command reports errors with a human-readable message. Add Route offers a route with metrics and options. Purge Route removes a previously offered route. Distance is included in the header as a hop count, incremented at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: RAP sends commands over TCP or UDP. Commands are simple: no-op, poll, error, add a route, or delete a route. Each command has a version number and length.

sections.title: Metrics and Policy Attributes
sections.content:
Routes in RAP carry optional metrics and policy attributes. Each metric or option begins with a 32-bit header specifying length, option class, format, and type. Metrics include Distance (hop count), Delay (path delay in seconds), MTU (minimum transmission unit in bytes), and Bandwidth (minimum path bandwidth in bytes/second).

Policy options include Origin (the router that created the route), Source Restriction (only use for packets from certain addresses), Destination Restriction (non-contiguous address masks), Trace (loop detection), AUP (Acceptable Use Policy), and Public (routes over public broadcast media). Routes can also carry cost metrics in various currencies, supporting tariff-based routing. Each option class (0 to 3) determines whether unknowns should be propagated, discarded, or treated as fatal.
sections.plainLanguage: Routes carry rich information: delay, bandwidth, who created it, who is allowed to use it, currency cost, and more. Different options have different rules about what to do if a router does not understand them.

sections.title: Processing, Filtering, and Aggregation
sections.content:
Incoming routes are filtered by proximity (distance and specificity), updated to reflect path metrics, aggregated to reduce routing table size, and selected for active use. Routes can then be offered to peers, subject to transmitter filtering and policy constraints.

Receiver filtering limits how far away routes are considered usable, based on distance and address mask specificity. Updates merge in new metrics: MTU and bandwidth are minimized over the path, delay and cost are summed, distance is incremented. Aggregation combines subset routes through the same peer into more general routes, reducing table bloat. Active route selection and transmitter filtering apply local policy to decide which routes to use and advertise.
sections.plainLanguage: Routes come in, get updated with new path information, combined when possible, and picked for use. Then they are offered to neighbors, obeying local rules about what to share.

sections.title: Loop Detection and Prevention
sections.content:
RAP relies on distance (hop count) as a last resort to prevent routing loops. Routers increment distance at each hop and discard routes where distance exceeds 2z + i, where z is the number of zero bits in the route's address mask and i is a small configurable number. This limit is much higher than RIP's fixed infinity of 15, allowing RAP to work at larger scales.

The Trace option offers active loop detection. When a router detects a route distance increasing twice in succession, it can add a trace option carrying its IP address. If a route arrives with its own trace already in it, the router purges the route, breaking the loop. Routers depend ultimately on distance to count out loops, even in the absence of trace detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers count hops to avoid loops. If a route gets too old (too many hops), it is thrown away. Routers can also mark routes with their address to detect and break loops faster.
